procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated March 30, 1966 of the Mysore High Court in Criminal Revision Petition No. 384 of 1965, which upheld the conviction of the appellants.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants were convicted in the trial court for an offence under s. 220 of the Mysore Village Panchayats and Local Boards Act, 1959. They then went to the Mysore High Court by way of Criminal Revision Petition No. 384 of 1965, contending that in view of Rule 16 of the Mysore Panchayat Secretaries' Powers and Duties Rules, 1961, they could not be prosecuted on a private complaint. The High Court rejected this argument, holding that Rule 16 did not preclude persons other than the Secretary from filing a complaint, but only debarred complaints being made by others on behalf of the Panchayat.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants, who were the Vice-Chairman and the Chairman of the Keladi village panchayat, appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's judgment. The issue before the Supreme Court was whether a private complaint could be entertained for the commission of an offence under s. 220 of the Mysore Village Panchayats & Local Boards Act, 1959.

issue.issue_text: Whether the interpretation put by the High Court on s. 200(1) of the Act was correct.

facts: The High Court interpreted s. 200(1) of the Act as an "enabling section."

According to the High Court, this section gave power to the Standing Committee and the Chief Officer to direct the initiation of proceedings, but it was not exhaustive, meaning other individuals could also file complaints for offenses under the Act.
law: The Supreme Court held that the interpretation of a statutory provision must consider the overall scheme of the Act and the purpose of the provision.
The word "may" in a statute does not necessarily mean that other methods are permitted; it can be used to grant discretion to a specified authority, rather than imposing a mandatory duty upon them.
application: The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court, stating that the scheme of the Act and the purpose of s. 200(1) make it clear that the legislature intended for proceedings to be instituted only in the manner laid down in that subsection.

The Court reasoned that the word "may" was used to give discretion to the Standing Committee or the Chief Officer to decide when to initiate proceedings, not to make it mandatory for them to do so in all cases.

It further argued that if the High Court's interpretation were correct, s. 200(1) would be "totally unnecessary," because there would be no need to specifically grant this power to certain officials if any private individual could file a complaint.

The Court rejected the idea that the provision was included merely for caution, questioning why, in that case, the power was limited to the Standing Committee and Chief Officer and not extended to others like the President of the Municipality.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's interpretation and held that any proceeding for an offense under the Act must be instituted exclusively in the manner laid down in s. 200(1) of the Act, and in no other way.

issue.issue_text: Whether all offences committed under the various provisions contained in the Act would be cognizable owing to the general powers conferred on police officers by s. 236 of the Act.

facts: The High Court held that all offences under the Act were cognizable.
The High Court based this conclusion on s. 236 of the Act, which grants a police officer the power to arrest any person committing an offence under the Act in their presence.
law: The Supreme Court observed that the Act itself distinguishes between cognizable and non-cognizable offences. For example, sections 15, 17, 21, and 22 expressly state that offences under them are cognizable, whereas sections 16, 18, 19, and 20 do not.

The Court cited legal authority for the principle that a limited power for a police officer to arrest someone for an offence committed in their presence does not, by itself, make that offence cognizable under the Criminal Procedure Code.
application: The Court reasoned that if the legislature had intended for all offences to be cognizable, it would not have specifically designated only certain sections as such.
The Court interpreted s. 236 as conferring only a "limited power" on the police, restricted to the specific circumstance of an offence being committed in the officer's presence.

This limited power of arrest is not equivalent to the general power to arrest without a warrant that characterizes a cognizable offence, which would also permit a full investigation and the filing of a charge sheet.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's view, concluding that s. 236 confers only a limited power of arrest and does not make all offences under the Act cognizable. The Court's reasoning was based on the fact that the Act itself explicitly differentiates between cognizable and non-cognizable offences, indicating a clear legislative intent that not all offences would be cognizable.

issue.issue_text: Whether a private complaint could be filed for the offence in question.

facts: A private complaint was filed against the appellants for an offence under s. 220 of the Mysore Village Panchayats and Local Boards Act, 1959.
The appellants contended that they could not be prosecuted on a private complaint because of a specific rule governing how complaints should be filed.
law: Rule 16 of the Mysore Panchayat Secretaries' Powers and Duties Rules, 1961, provided that the Secretary shall have the power to file complaints and suits on behalf of the Panchayat.
application: The Court determined that the Panchayat is the entity primarily interested in taking action against its members for contraventions of the Act.

It examined the overall "scheme of the Act," particularly sections 214 to 219, which deal with infractions of Panchayat orders. This scheme indicated that the legislature did not contemplate complaints being filed by private individuals.

The Court reasoned that the existence of a specific rule (Rule 16) empowering the Secretary to file complaints on behalf of the Panchayat implies that this is the exclusive method. If any private individual could file a complaint, this rule would be unnecessary.

The Court dismissed the High Court's concern that a Secretary might be embarrassed to file a complaint against a superior, stating that the Secretary acts on behalf of the Panchayat, and the question of subordination is irrelevant.
Following the reasoning in a previous case, the Court held that when a statute lays down a specific manner for instituting proceedings, it must be done in that manner only.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that based on Rule 16 and the overall scheme of the Act, only the Secretary of the Panchayat was competent to file the complaint. Therefore, the private complaint was not maintainable and was rejected.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the interpretation put by the High Court on s. 200(1) of the Act was correct.
appellant_arguments: The interpretation of s. 200(1) by the High Court is incorrect.
The provision is not merely enabling but is exhaustive, meaning only the authorities specified (like the Standing Committee or the Chief Officer) can direct the filing of a complaint.
This position is supported by the precedent set in K. M. Kanavi v. State of Mysore, which dealt with similar provisions.
respondent_arguments: Section 200(1) is an enabling section that gives power to the Standing Committee and the Chief Officer to direct proceedings.
It is not exhaustive and does not preclude other authorities or individuals from initiating proceedings.
There is no specific provision in the Act that forbids a court from taking cognizance of an offence except on a complaint made under the direction of the specified authorities.

arguments.issue_text: Whether all offences committed under the various provisions contained in the Act would be cognizable owing to the general powers conferred on police officers by s. 236 of the Act.
appellant_arguments: Section 236 of the Act does not make all offences under the Act cognizable.
The section confers only a limited power on the police, not a general power to investigate all offences under the Act as cognizable.
respondent_arguments: All offences under the Act are cognizable because of the general powers granted to police officers under s. 236 of the Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a private complaint could be filed for the offence in question.
appellant_arguments: A private complaint is not maintainable for offences under this Act.
The scheme of the Act, supported by Rule 16, indicates that only a designated authority (in this case, the Secretary of the Panchayat) is competent to file a complaint.
respondent_arguments: A private complaint is maintainable as there is no explicit bar in the Act against it.

cases.case_name: K. M. Kanavi v. State of Mysore
cases.principle: Where a statute provides a specific authority for initiating proceedings for an offence (in that case, a complaint made under a direction of the Standing Committee or the Chief Officer), that provision is exhaustive and mandatory, not merely enabling, and it precludes complaints from being filed by others.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where a statute provides that a specific authority 'may' direct the institution of proceedings for an offense, this procedure is exclusive. The word 'may' confers discretion on that authority as to whether to initiate proceedings, but it does not permit proceedings to be instituted by any other person or in any other manner.
obiter: A statutory provision granting a police officer the power to arrest a person committing an offense in their presence does not, by itself, make all offenses under that statute cognizable.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Based on the precedent set in K. M. Kanavi's case, which dealt with similar statutory provisions, the court held that the power to file a complaint under the Act was exclusive to the designated authority. The court reasoned that if any private individual could institute proceedings, the specific provision empowering the Standing Committee or Chief Officer (in the precedent case) or the Secretary (in the present case) would be "totally unnecessary." Therefore, if a proceeding for punishment is to be instituted, it must be done in the manner laid down by the specific rule—in this case, by the Secretary of the Panchayat under Rule 16—and in that manner only.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory Scheme Interpretation: The court analyzed the "scheme of the Act" as a whole, rather than isolated provisions, to determine that the legislature intended for proceedings to be instituted only in the specified manner, stating "the scheme of the Act and the purpose of this provision... makes it clear that the legislature intended that such proceedings should only be instituted in the manner laid down in that sub-section."

Canon Against Surplusage: The court reasoned that interpreting the provision as merely enabling and not exclusive would render it redundant. "If the interpretation put by the High Court on this provision is accepted, it would mean that this provision was totally unnecessary, because there would be no need to confer power on the Standing Committee or the Chief Officer to make such directions if such directions could be made or proceedings instituted at the instance of any private individual."

Application of Precedent (Stare Decisis): The court explicitly followed the ratio of its previous decision in K. M. Kanavi v. State of Mysore, stating, "Following the ratio of the above decision it would be legitimate to hold that the complaint, in the present case, could be filed under Rule 16 only by the Secretary of the Panchayat and by no one else."
policy_considerations: The court dismissed the practical concern that a subordinate Secretary might find it embarrassing to file a complaint against a superior, like the Chairman. It reasoned that this difficulty "can hardly be accepted as serious" because the Secretary's duty is to the Panchayat as an institution, not to individual office bearers. The court clarified, "The Secretary has to act on behalf of the Panchayat and it is the panchayat that would be vitally interested in preventing and stopping any contravention... The question of his subordination to any one of its office bearera is of no consequence."
